two-way automata are equivalent to two-way automata equipped with a pushdown store and a nonerasing stack, that two-way automaton with a pushdown stack can be simulated by a two-way automaton equipped with an arbitrary number of nonerasing stacks, and that the latter class is equivalent to two-way Turing automata with one nonerasing stack.
two-way automata equipped with a stack and checking stacks can simulate Turing machines with a linear number of tapes, and that the corresponding restricted classes are closed under complementation.
the computational power of these automata is determined by the following three factors: (1) the number of checking tapes, (2) the number of stack symbols, and (3) the number of states.

the computational power of all the considered automata is the same as the power of two-way Turing machines.
two-way automata are as powerful as Turing machines if the automata are equipped with a stack and an arbitrary number (possibly zero) of checking stacks.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
two-way automata are able to accept elementary sets if they are equipped with a stack or an arbitrary number of stacks.
the computational power of these restricted classes of two-way automaton is not very much influenced by the number of storage media used.

the computational power of a restricted two-way automaton with one subrecursive storage device and an arbitrary number (possibly zero) of checking stacks can be characterized by the time and space complexity class defined by the corresponding subrecursive storage device.

the computational power of these automata can be characterized in terms which are more natural and intuitive than in terms of the elementary hierarchy.
two-way automata can be equipped with an arbitrary number of subrecursive storage devices and still maintain their computational strength.
